title: Qualified SR&ED Expenditures - Canadian Tax Credit Glossary
description: Review our Canadian SR&ED glossary to learn what counts as Qualified SR&ED Expenditures when calculating your R&D investment tax credit claim.
summary: Qualified SR&ED expenditures are the costs that earn Canada's federal Scientific Research and Experimental Development investment tax credit under subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act. They differ from the section 37 deduction pool: arm's-length contracts count at 80%, the 55% proxy amount is added, and assistance reduces them dollar-for-dollar. Qualifying CCPCs earn 35% on up to CA$6.0 million.

body.text: Qualified SR&ED expenditures are the costs that earn Canada's federal Scientific Research and Experimental Development investment tax credit under subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act. They differ from the section 37 deduction pool: arm's-length contracts count at 80%, the 55% proxy amount is added, and assistance reduces them dollar-for-dollar. Qualifying CCPCs earn 35% on up to CA$6.0 million.

Canada operates one of the largest and most technically rigorous research and development (R&D) tax incentive frameworks in the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), anchored federally by the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program. Delivering approximately CA$4.5 billion annually in federal tax assistance, the SR&ED program functions alongside a comprehensive matrix of provincial and territorial R&D tax credits and direct federal innovation grants.

Between December 2024 and October 2026, Canada's federal and provincial R&D tax landscape underwent its most significant structural overhaul since the 2012–2014 federal reforms. Federally, Bill C-15 (Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, enacted sweeping legislative enhancements retroactive to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (that is, on or after December 16, 2024). Bill C-15 doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% refundable Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from CA$3.0 million to CA$6.0 million (yielding up to CA$2.1 million in annual refundable federal credits and superseding the interim CA$4.5 million proposal in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement), expanded the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from CA$10 million–CA$50 million to CA$15 million–CA$75 million, introduced an elective 3-year average gross revenue phase-out test over the same CA$15 million–CA$75 million range, extended the enhanced 35% refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), and fully reinstated the eligibility of SR&ED capital expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024. Administratively, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval Process on April 1, 2026, utilizing Form T1322 to provide upfront technical eligibility determinations within eight weeks and halving post-filing expenditure review service standards from 180 calendar days to 90 calendar days.

Concurrently, major provincial jurisdictions restructured their innovation tax regimes. In Québec, the 2025–2026 Budget Plan tabled on March 25, 2025, abolished eight legacy innovation tax measures—including the four historical R&D tax credits for salaries, university research, pre-competitive private partnerships, and research consortia—and consolidated them into the new Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, offering a 30% refundable credit on the first CA$1.0 million of eligible R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures (including capital equipment) above an exclusion threshold, and 20% thereafter. In Ontario, the provincial government harmonized the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC, 8% refundable) and the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC, 3.5% non-refundable) with the federal restoration of capital expenditures effective December 16, 2024, while retaining Ontario's existing CA$3.0 million annual OITC expenditure cap. In Saskatchewan, the refundable ceiling for Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) under the 10% Saskatchewan R&D Tax Credit doubled from CA$1.0 million to CA$2.0 million of eligible expenditures for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024.
Section 1: Statutory and Legislative Architecture of the Federal SR&ED Program
1.1 Dual-Mechanism Statutory Structure in the Income Tax Act

Unlike single-instrument R&D tax regimes that provide either a super-deduction or a standalone tax credit, the federal SR&ED program under the Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (the "Act" or "ITA"), and Part XXIX (section 2900 et seq.) of the Income Tax Regulations, C.R.C., c. 945 (the "Regulations" or "ITR"), operates through two distinct, sequential statutory calculations:

items: The Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures: Governed by subsection 37(1) of the Act, this mechanism aggregates allowable current and (for property acquired after December 15, 2024) capital SR&ED expenditures incurred in Canada into a cumulative tax deduction pool. Taxpayers may deduct any portion of the positive pool balance in computing net business income for the current taxation year or carry the undeducted pool balance forward indefinitely to offset business income in future taxation years.

The Section 127 and Section 127.1 Investment Tax Credit (ITC): Governed by subsections 127(5) through 127(36) and section 127.1 of the Act, this mechanism calculates a volume-based Investment Tax Credit (at either the 15% basic rate or the 35% enhanced rate) on the taxpayer's "qualified expenditures" defined in subsection 127(9). Depending on the claimant's legal status and expenditure type, unused ITCs may offset Part I federal income tax payable, generate an immediate cash refund under subsection 127.1(1), or be carried back 3 taxation years and forward up to 20 taxation years.

body.text: A foundational principle of Canadian tax auditing is that an "allowable SR&ED expenditure" deductible under section 37 and a "qualified expenditure" eligible for an ITC under subsection 127(9) are not interchangeable terms. For example, under the Proxy Method, the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) calculated under Regulation 2900(4) is added to subsection 127(9) qualified expenditures to generate an ITC, but is strictly excluded from the section 37 deduction pool. Conversely, payments to a non-arm's length (NAL) SR&ED subcontractor are 100% includable in the payer's section 37 deduction pool under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01), but are 0% includable in the payer's subsection 127(9) qualified expenditures unless the NAL performer transfers its qualified expenditures via a joint agreement on Form T1146 pursuant to subsection 127(13). Similarly, for arm's-length SR&ED contracts and third-party payments, 100% of the eligible outlay enters the section 37 pool, whereas only 80% enters subsection 127(9) qualified expenditures.
1.2 The Statutory Definition of SR&ED under Subsection 248(1)

The gateway to all federal and provincial R&D tax incentives in Canada is the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" codified in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act (which was moved from Regulation 2900(1) to the Act without altering the applicability of the judicial test, as confirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal in Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88). Under subsection 248(1), SR&ED is defined as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" and that falls within one of four inclusive branches (paragraphs (a) to (d)), subject to seven absolute statutory exclusions (paragraphs (e) to (k)).

The first inclusive branch, Basic Research (paragraph 248(1)(a)), encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. Basic research typically occurs in laboratory settings, may be published in scientific journals, and seeks to expand the existing scientific knowledge base. The second branch, Applied Research (paragraph 248(1)(b)), covers work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. While directed toward a practical objective (such as developing a vaccine against a newly discovered virus by exploiting its characteristics), applied research still pursues the advancement of scientific knowledge.

The third and primary industrial branch, Experimental Development (paragraph 248(1)(c)), encompasses work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Crucially, the statute explicitly protects incremental technological improvements: a taxpayer does not need to produce a commercially successful or world-first product, provided the work seeks to generate or discover new technological knowledge or know-how that resolves an underlying technological uncertainty.

The fourth branch, Eligible Support Work (paragraph 248(1)(d)), covers work with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, where that work is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of work described in paragraph (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada. This eight-item enumeration in paragraph (d) is a closed statutory list. Support work does not constitute SR&ED on its own; its eligibility is strictly derivative of, and commensurate (corresponding in amount, size, extent, or duration) with, the basic research, applied research, or experimental development that it directly supports.
Statutory Exclusions under Paragraphs 248(1)(e) to (k)

Even where a project involves genuine experimental development, any activities falling within paragraphs (e) to (k) of the subsection 248(1) definition are statutorily excluded from SR&ED and cannot be claimed:

items: Paragraph 248(1)(e): Market research or sales promotion (work that supplements advertising and personal selling).
Paragraph 248(1)(f): Quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes.
Paragraph 248(1)(g): Research in the social sciences or the humanities (which catches many commercial data analytics projects).
Paragraph 248(1)(h): Prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas.
Paragraph 248(1)(i): The commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process.
Paragraph 248(1)(j): Style changes.
Paragraph 248(1)(k): Routine data collection.

body.text: As the CRA's Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives emphasize, the key feature that distinguishes eligible support work under paragraph (d) (such as "data collection" or "testing") from excluded work under paragraphs (f) and (k) ("routine testing" or "routine data collection") is purpose. If data collection or testing is carried out specifically for the purpose of performing SR&ED (to test a hypothesis and resolve a scientific or technological uncertainty), it qualifies as paragraph (d) support work; if it is done for normal business operations or standard quality assurance, it is statutorily excluded. Furthermore, acquiring existing available knowledge or know-how—such as through employee training, on-the-job learning, hiring expert employees or consultants to apply knowledge they already possess, or purchasing proprietary knowledge—does not meet the requirement of attempting to achieve scientific or technological advancement and is non-claimable.

body.text: 1.4 Legislative Evolution: 2024 Fall Economic Statement, Budget 2025, and Bill C-15
Auditors reviewing Canadian R&D tax documentation from 2024 through 2026 must carefully distinguish between interim policy announcements and the final enacted law in Bill C-15:

items: The 2024 Fall Economic Statement (December 16, 2024): Tabled on December 16, 2024, the 2024 Fall Economic Statement initially proposed raising the enhanced 35% ITC expenditure limit from CA$3.0 million to CA$4.5 million, increasing the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from CA$10 million–CA$50 million to CA$15 million–CA$75 million, extending the 35% enhanced rate to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) using a 3-year average gross revenue phase-out over CA$15 million–CA$75 million, and restoring the eligibility of capital expenditures and equipment lease costs for SR&ED, all effective for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024 (or property acquired and lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024).

Federal Budget 2025 (November 4, 2025): Tabled on November 4, 2025, Budget 2025 confirmed all of the 2024 Fall Economic Statement SR&ED proposals and expanded upon them by raising the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% credit from the previously announced CA$4.5 million to CA$6.0 million, retroactive to taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024. Budget 2025 estimated the incremental fiscal cost of increasing the limit from CA$4.5 million to CA$6.0 million at CA$293 million over five fiscal years (CA$3 million in 2025–2026, CA$70 million in 2026–2027, CA$85 million in 2027–2028, CA$65 million in 2028–2029, and CA$70 million in 2029–2030). Budget 2025 also announced administrative modernization effective April 1, 2026, including an elective Pre-Claim Approval Process, greater use of artificial intelligence in program administration, and a streamlined review process cutting expenditure review processing times in half from 180 days to 90 days.

Enactment of Bill C-15 (March 26, 2026): Parliament enacted the Budget 2025 and 2024 Fall Economic Statement SR&ED reforms through Bill C-15 (Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Consequently, any secondary literature citing a CA$3.0 million or CA$4.5 million federal expenditure limit for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, is statutorily outdated; the legally enacted ceiling is CA$6.0 million. Following Royal Assent, the CRA published revised Form T661 (May 15, 2026), T2 Schedule 31 (May 22, 2026), T2 Schedule 49 (May 29, 2026), Form T1145 (May 15, 2026), Form T1146 (May 15, 2026), and updated administrative policies for Capital Expenditures (June 29, 2026), Lease Expenditures (June 8, 2026), Shared-Use Equipment (May 22, 2026), Total Qualified Expenditures (May 22, 2026), and Investment Tax Credits (October 7, 2026).

body.text: 2.2 Entity Classification, Rate Tiers, and Refundability Rules
The rate of the federal SR&ED ITC and whether unused credits can be converted into a direct cash refund depend on the legal classification of the claimant and the nature of the expenditure.

Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) earn the enhanced 35% ITC (15% basic rate plus 20% enhancement) on qualified expenditures up to their available annual Expenditure Limit (baseline CA$6,000,000 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024). For a qualifying CCPC, unused ITCs earned at the 35% enhanced rate are 100% refundable on current expenditures and the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA), and 40% refundable on eligible SR&ED capital expenditures acquired after December 15, 2024. Qualified expenditures incurred by a CCPC in excess of its annual expenditure limit earn the 15% basic ITC.

Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) gained access under Bill C-15, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, to the enhanced 35% ITC on up to CA$6,000,000 of qualified expenditures, with 100% refundability on current expenditures and the PPA and 40% refundability on eligible capital expenditures. This measure also extends to Canadian-resident subsidiaries wholly or substantially owned by eligible Canadian public corporations.

Other Corporations (Non-CCPCs and Large Public Corporations) that do not qualify as a CCPC or an ECPC—or that have phased out of the expenditure limit—earn the 15% non-refundable basic ITC on all qualified SR&ED expenditures without an expenditure ceiling. These non-refundable ITCs may be applied to reduce federal Part I income tax payable to zero, carried back 3 taxation years, or carried forward 20 taxation years.

Individuals (Sole Proprietorships) and Trusts earn the 15% basic ITC on qualified SR&ED expenditures (claimed on Form T2038(IND)). While practitioner summaries note that sole proprietorships and trusts earn the 15% rate and generally apply credits against tax payable or carry them forward, the CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy notes that detailed entity-specific provisions in the Act govern partial refundability for qualifying unincorporated claimants.

Partnerships (SR&ED Claims for Partnerships Policy) are subject to distinct flow-through rules because a partnership is not a person or taxpayer under subsection 96(1) of the Act and cannot earn an ITC or receive a cash refund in its own right:

items: Mandatory Current-Year Pool Deduction: The entire balance of the partnership's section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures must be deducted in full in computing partnership net income in the fiscal period incurred; a partnership cannot carry forward a section 37 pool to future years.

15% Rate Cap on Partnership ITCs: The SR&ED ITC is computed at the partnership level solely at the 15% basic rate—even if the partners are CCPCs—and allocated at the end of the partnership's fiscal period to eligible partners under subsection 127(8). Furthermore, the partnership's section 37 pool is reduced in the same fiscal period by the ITCs allocated to the partners under subsection 127(12.1), regardless of whether a partner has claimed the ITC against Part I tax or received a refund.

Prohibition on Allocation to Specified Members (Limited Partners): Under subsection 127(8), no SR&ED ITC may be allocated to a "specified member" of the partnership (defined in subsection 248(1) as any limited partner under subsection 96(2.4) or any general partner who was not regularly, continuously, and substantially actively engaged in the partnership's business activities other than financing). In addition, a partnership loss created or increased by deducting the section 37 SR&ED pool is not allowed to a limited partner.

Reallocation and Form T932 Renunciation: ITCs that cannot be allocated to specified members may be reasonably reallocated to active non-specified general partners, who may elect to renounce any part of those reallocated ITCs using Form T932 (Election by a Member of a Partnership to Renounce Investment Tax Credits Pursuant to Subsection 127(8.4)) so that the renounced ITCs are extinguished and do not reduce the partnership's section 37 deductible pool.

body.text: 2.3 Expenditure Limit Phase-Out Formulas (Taxable Capital vs. Gross Revenue)

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the baseline CA$6,000,000 expenditure limit for the 35% enhanced ITC is subject to two alternative phase-out mechanisms under subsections 127(10.2) through 127(10.64).
1. The Taxable Capital Phase-Out Formula (Default for CCPCs — ITA s. 127(10.2))

Unless a CCPC (and all CCPCs in its associated group under section 256) elects to use the revenue method, its annual expenditure limit decreases linearly as the combined taxable capital employed in Canada (as defined for Part I.3 tax purposes; see archived CRA Interpretation Bulletin IT-532) of the CCPC and all associated CCPCs for the immediately preceding taxation year increases from CA$15,000,000 to CA$75,000,000:

In this formula, A is nil if the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada of the corporation (and associated CCPCs) is less than or equal to CA$15,000,000, and otherwise equals the lesser of CA$60,000,000 and the amount by which prior-year taxable capital exceeds CA$15,000,000. Thus, the expenditure limit begins to decrease once prior-year taxable capital reaches CA$15,000,000 and becomes nil (CA$0) when prior-year taxable capital reaches CA$75,000,000. (For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the CA$3,000,000 expenditure limit phased out between CA$10,000,000 and CA$50,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital using a CA$40,000,000 denominator.) Associated CCPCs must allocate the shared expenditure limit among group members using Schedule T2SCH49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit) under subsections 127(10.21) and 127(10.3).
2. The 3-Year Average Gross Revenue Phase-Out Formula (Mandatory for ECPCs; Elective for CCPCs — ITA s. 127(10.6))

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) must calculate their expenditure limit using the revenue method under subsections 127(10.6) to 127(10.64). Additionally, a CCPC may elect to use this revenue method instead of the taxable capital method, provided that if the CCPC is part of an associated group, all CCPCs in the associated group jointly elect using the prescribed schedule.

Under the revenue method, the CA$6,000,000 expenditure limit is reduced linearly based on the average annual gross revenue over the 3 preceding fiscal years—as reflected in the consolidated financial statements of the consolidated group for ECPCs, or the combined financial statements of all associated group members for electing CCPCs, regardless of whether the corporations were associated throughout the entire 3-year period—over the exact same CA$15,000,000 to CA$75,000,000 range, becoming nil when 3-year average annual revenue reaches CA$75,000,000 or greater.
2.4 Mechanics of the Section 37 Pool and Next-Year Taxability of ITCs

A common error in financial modelling of Canadian SR&ED claims is treating the 35% or 15% federal ITC as a tax-free windfall. Under the Income Tax Act, federal SR&ED ITCs that are claimed (either applied to reduce Part I tax payable or received as a cash refund) are included in taxable income in the following taxation year through the mechanics of the section 37 pool:

items: Year 1 Claim: In Taxation Year 1, the claimant incurs CA$1,000,000 of current SR&ED expenditures, deducts the full CA$1,000,000 from business income under subsection 37(1) (leaving a closing section 37 pool balance of CA$0 on Line 470 of Form T661), and earns a CA$350,000 refundable federal ITC.

Year 2 Pool Reduction (ITA s. 37(1)(e)): In Taxation Year 2, paragraph 37(1)(e) requires the claimant to reduce its section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures by the CA$350,000 ITC applied or refunded in Taxation Year 1 (reported on Line 435 of Form T661).

Income Inclusion if Pool is Negative (ITA s. 12(1)(v)): If the claimant incurs at least CA$350,000 of net new SR&ED expenditures in Year 2, the Year 1 ITC simply reduces the deductible Year 2 section 37 pool by CA$350,000. If, however, the claimant incurs zero SR&ED expenditures in Year 2 (or less than CA$350,000), the closing section 37 pool balance becomes negative, and paragraph 12(1)(v) mandates that the negative balance be included directly in computing the claimant's net business income for Year 2. That included amount is then added back to the pool under paragraph 37(1)(c.1) so that the opening section 37 pool balance for Year 3 resets to nil (CA$0).

body.text: 3.2 The Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) and Salary Base Restrictions

Under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations, the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is equal to 55% of the claimant's eligible salary base. Auditors must reject any claim or advisory document applying a 65% proxy rate (which applied only in 2012 and earlier) or a 60% rate (which applied only in 2013); since 2014, the statutory rate under Regulation 2900(4) has been fixed at 55%.
1. Computing the Part 5 Salary Base (Regulations 2900(4), 2900(5), and 2900(9))

The salary base calculated in Part 5, Section A of Form T661 is narrower than the allowable SR&ED salaries and wages reported in Part 3, Section B. Under Regulation 2900(9), for any employee (whether a specified employee or not), the salary base cannot include any of the following five categories (which are subtracted on Line 812 for non-specified employees and excluded from Box 852 for specified employees):

items: Taxable benefits under section 6 or stock option benefits under section 7 of the Act.
Unpaid remuneration from a prior taxation year that was paid in the current taxation year (reported on Line 310 of Form T661).
Remuneration based on profits.
Bonuses.
Related benefits (the employer's share of contributions to the Canada Pension Plan [CPP], Employment Insurance [EI], and similar payroll levies).

body.text: 2. Statutory Caps on Specified Employees (Regulations 2900(7), 2900(8), and 2900(10))

For a specified employee (shareholder-employee), the amount of eligible salary or wages that can be included in the Part 5 proxy salary base (Box 860 of Form T661) is restricted under subsection 2900(7) of the Regulations to the lesser of two statutory limits:

items: The 75% Time Cap (Box 854 / Box 856): 75% of the specified employee's total annual salary or wages from the employer (both SR&ED and non-SR&ED, excluding bonuses, profit-based remuneration, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year in Box 852), calculated by multiplying Box 852 by the percentage of time spent directly on SR&ED up to a maximum of 75% (Box 854).

The 2.5 × YMPE Statutory Ceiling (Box 858): An absolute dollar limit equal to 2.5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) (determined under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan) for the calendar year in which the claimant's taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year that the claimant employed the individual:

body.text: Maximum Specified Employee Proxy Salary Base = 2.5 × A × (B / 365)

In this formula, A is the YMPE (the first earnings ceiling under the CPP, not the Year's Additional Maximum Pensionable Earnings [YAMPE / CPP2] introduced in 2024) for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, and B is the number of days in the taxation year that the claimant employed the individual (with no proration for any portion of the year during which the individual was not a specified employee).

body.text: Under Regulations 2900(8) and 2900(10), if a specified employee is employed by two or more associated corporations (including related individuals or partnerships deemed to be associated corporations under Regulation 2900(10)) whose taxation years end in the same calendar year, the combined proxy salary base claimed across the entire associated group for that individual cannot exceed 2.5 × YMPE, and the associated corporations must file an allocation agreement on Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED)).
3. The Overall Cap on the PPA (Regulation 2900(6))

Under subsection 2900(6) of the Regulations, the Prescribed Proxy Amount cannot exceed the claimant's Overall Cap, which ensures that the PPA and other specific deductions do not exceed total business expenditures deducted in the taxation year. The Overall Cap is calculated as:
Overall Cap = A − B − C

In this formula, A equals the total amounts deducted in calculating net business income for tax purposes for the year (including cost of goods sold); B equals the total deductions claimed in the year under sections 20 (such as Capital Cost Allowance [CCA], interest, and bad debts), 24 (ceasing to carry on a business), 26 (banks), 30 (improving land for farming), 32 (insurance agents or brokers), 37 (SR&ED expenditures), 66 to 66.8 (resource exploration and development expenses), and 104 (trusts); and C equals the amount of expenditures incurred for the use of, or the right to use, a building. As the CRA's Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy confirms, the Overall Cap generally does not restrict the 55% PPA if the claimant has deducted more than CA$55 of non-SR&ED operating expenses (excluding building rent and the statutory deductions in B) for every CA$100 of eligible salary included in the salary base.
3.3 Detailed Eligibility Rules for Specific Expenditure Categories
1. Salaries and Wages (ITA s. 248(1), s. 37(1)(a)(i), s. 78(4), CRA SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy)

Allowable salaries and wages include the portion of income from an office or employment (subdivision a of Division B of Part I of the Act) reasonably related to hands-on SR&ED work performed in Canada. Directly engaged tasks include experimentation and analysis, the eight categories of paragraph 248(1)(d) support work, certain tasks performed by non-specialized employees supervised by staff with scientific or technological qualifications (such as operating a machine required for an experiment or feeding raw materials into a machine), direct technical supervision of SR&ED employees, technical input into SR&ED contract administration, technological planning for ongoing SR&ED projects claimed in the year (personnel assignment, job priorities, technological strategies, material quality), technological feasibility studies, and internal technical documentation. Under the All or Substantially All (ASA) Rule, for employees who spend 90% or more of their time on the prosecution of SR&ED, 100% of their eligible salary or wages is considered to relate to SR&ED.

With respect to bonuses, profit-based remuneration, and dividends, bonuses or remuneration based on profits paid or payable to a specified employee cannot be included as SR&ED salary or wages expenditures. For employees who are not specified employees, bonuses and profit-based remuneration can be included in Part 3 SR&ED wages (Line 300) only if they have a reasonable link to the prosecution of SR&ED (such as an enforceable bonus paid out of normal ongoing operational business income), and are excluded if earned from capital transactions (sale of a business, shares, or assets), finder's fees, or achieving sales targets. Dividends are not salary or wages and cannot be claimed, and stock option benefits, retiring allowances, and the employer's share of related benefits are excluded from direct SR&ED wages. Where taxable benefits included on an employee's T4 slip include a GST/HST or PST component for which the employer can claim an input tax credit or rebate, that input tax credit is deemed to be government assistance under subsection 248(16) and must be excluded from allowable SR&ED wages.

Under the 180-Day Unpaid Remuneration Rule (ITA s. 78(4)), employee remuneration incurred in a taxation year that is not paid within 180 days after the end of that taxation year is deemed not to have been incurred in that year. Unpaid amounts must be subtracted on Line 315 of Form T661 in the year incurred and can be claimed on Line 310 in the subsequent taxation year in which they are actually paid.

For SR&ED Work Performed Outside Canada (Lines 307 and 309), permissible salary or wages qualify only if all five statutory criteria are satisfied: (1) the work was done directly by an employee and not a contractor; (2) the employee was a resident of Canada at the time the expense was incurred; (3) the work related to a business of the claimant; (4) the work was an integral part and solely in support of SR&ED carried out in Canada by the claimant; and (5) the salary or wages are not subject to income or profits tax from another country. The maximum allowable claim for outside-Canada wages is capped at 10% of the total SR&ED salary or wages for SR&ED carried on in Canada (Line 306 of Form T661).
2. Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed (ITA s. 37(1)(a)(i), ITR s. 2900(2)(a))

Under the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy, "materials for SR&ED" refers to physical, tangible raw materials, substances, or other items (existing in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state) that compose the body of a thing at a given moment in the SR&ED process—either a tangible object on which SR&ED is being carried out, or a tangible object that results from the SR&ED. Cost is determined on a laid-down basis (invoice cost plus customs and excise duties, transportation, storage, and acquisition costs, or manufactured inventory cost including direct labour and production overhead) and can only be claimed in the taxation year in which the material is consumed or transformed in SR&ED in Canada (never when merely purchased into inventory), and must be paid within the taxation year or within 180 days of year-end to earn an ITC.

Materials Consumed (Line 320) are materials destroyed or rendered virtually valueless as a result of the SR&ED (such as cardboard boxes destroyed during printing process tests, ink, seeds, growth media, agar, fungal cultures, animal feed, plant fertilizers, pesticides, herbicides, and fungicides). Materials consumed are not subject to ITC recapture unless proceeds received exceed 10% of cost. Materials Transformed (Line 325) are materials changed or incorporated into another material, experimental product, custom product, or commercial asset that retains some value. Laboratory supplies that do not compose the body of the object (such as petri dishes, beakers, flasks, pipettes, cleaning supplies, CDs/DVDs, and used lubricants) and general utilities (water, electricity, gas, propane, unless the energy itself is the direct subject of the SR&ED) do not qualify as materials, though they may qualify as overhead on Line 360 under the Traditional Method.

Under the SR&ED During Production Runs Policy, when experimental development occurs in a pilot plant or where technical risk to the process or product precludes simultaneous commercial work, the run is Experimental Development + Experimental Production (ED+EP), and the cost of materials consumed or transformed in the required experimental production is allowable (excluding any "excess production" beyond what is required for SR&ED validation). When experimental development occurs simultaneously with commercial production without technical risk to quality or stability (Experimental Development + Commercial Production [ED+CP]), only the additional (incremental) costs of materials consumed or transformed (such as actual material loss minus standard commercial material loss) are allowable. Where isolating SR&ED costs in an ED+CP run is impossible, the CRA may accept an alternative incremental cost calculation (Actual ED+CP run costs − Standard commercial production costs) provided the CRA agrees and the claimant signs a waiver of its right to object or appeal under subsection 169(2.2). Similarly, under the SR&ED while Developing an Asset Policy, when developing a custom product (for sale) or a commercial asset (for internal business use), claimants cannot claim all materials of the entire commercial asset and rely on ITC recapture later; only the materials consumed or transformed in the specific components requiring SR&ED (and closely associated redesigned components) are allowable.
3. Subcontractors (SR&ED Contracts) vs. Third-Party Payments

4. Overhead, Cloud Computing, and Prescribed Expenditures (ITR s. 2900(2)(c), s. 2900(3), s. 2902)

Under the Traditional Method (Line 360), an expenditure of a current nature qualifies under Regulation 2900(2)(c) only if it satisfies two mandatory tests: (1) it is directly related to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (meaning a direct linkage with no intervening step or intermediary between the expenditure and the SR&ED work, the SR&ED staff, or the machinery/equipment used by staff to perform SR&ED); and (2) it is incremental (meaning the expenditure would not have been incurred had such prosecution of SR&ED not occurred). Additionally, Regulation 2900(3) allows the cost of maintenance and upkeep of SR&ED premises, facilities, or equipment (though fixed-cost maintenance contracts generally fail the incremental test).

Regarding cloud computing, software, and utilities, under the Proxy Method, cloud computing costs are not claimable as separate expenses because the 55% PPA replaces direct overhead claims. Under the Traditional Method, utilities and incremental communications charges directly tied to SR&ED are allowable on Line 360, whereas fixed monthly internet/telephone plans fail the incremental test. Purchased software licences and capital data sets are capital expenditures rather than Regulation 2900(2)(a) materials; outside of SR&ED, purchased application software is 100% deductible in CCA Class 12, and computer hardware and systems software fall in CCA Class 50 (55% normal rate, enhanced to a 100% immediate first-year write-off for property acquired after April 15, 2024, and available for use before January 1, 2027).

Under Regulation 2902, prescribed expenditures are excluded from qualified expenditures even under the Traditional Method, including general administration or management expenses, legal or accounting fees (cl. 2902(a)(i)(B) — which bars SR&ED claim preparation fees), interest and borrowing costs (cl. 2902(a)(i)(C)), conventions and conferences (cl. 2902(a)(i)(F), even if technical), entertainment, advertising/selling expenses, dues/memberships, and fines/penalties. Similarly, headhunter fees, hiring advertisements, interview travel, and work-permit/immigration costs are non-allowable regular business expenses, whereas domestic moving expenses to relocate selected candidates or transfer SR&ED staff to another facility within Canada can qualify on Line 360 under the Traditional Method.
3.4 Restored Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)
Bill C-15 restored the eligibility of SR&ED capital expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment, and equipment lease costs for property acquired or leased after December 15, 2024:

items: SR&ED Capital Expenditures (ITA s. 37(1)(b), s. 127(9), CRA SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy — Updated June 29, 2026):

Depreciable property (other than a building or a leasehold interest in a building, land, inventory, or goodwill) acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024 (subsection 37(1.2)) qualifies as both a section 37 deductible expenditure (Line 390 of Form T661, with up to the 10 most expensive properties and their % SR&ED operating time listed on Lines 262 and 263) and a subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure for ITC purposes, provided that at the time of acquisition the claimant intended either (a) to use the property during all or substantially all (ASA, 90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life in SR&ED in Canada, or (b) to consume ASA (90% or more) of its value in SR&ED in Canada.

While used depreciable property can be included in the section 37 deductible pool, used equipment is a prescribed expenditure under Regulation 2902(b) and does not earn an ITC unless refurbished by the vendor prior to acquisition so significantly that it is brought to the current state of the art and considered new when acquired (or if refurbished by the claimant after December 15, 2024, in which case only the refurbishment costs qualify for the ITC).

For qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs earning the 35% enhanced ITC on capital property, the credit is 40% refundable. Capital expenditures claimed on Line 390 of Form T661 must not be claimed for Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) on Schedule T2SCH8.
Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) (ITA s. 127(9), ITR s. 2900(11), CRA SR&ED Shared-Use Equipment Policy — Updated May 22, 2026):

New depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024, that does not meet the 90% ASA test can qualify as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) under both the Traditional and Proxy methods if it is not Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under Regulation 2900(11), is not general-purpose office equipment or furniture (GPOEF), and is actually used primarily (more than 50% but less than 90% of its actual operating time) for SR&ED in Canada.

The capital cost remains on Schedule T2SCH8 for regular CCA depreciation (and is excluded from the section 37 pool), while the claimant includes 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost (excluding borrowed money under section 21) on Line 504 (Box 792) as a qualified expenditure for First-Term SUE at the end of the first taxation year ending at least 12 months after acquisition, and a second 1/4 (25%) for Second-Term SUE at the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months after acquisition. Any SUE ITC claimed or refunded reduces the Schedule 8 Undepreciated Capital Cost (UCC) in the subsequent year.
Equipment Lease Expenditures (ITA s. 37(8)(a)(ii), CRA SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy — Updated June 8, 2026):

For equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, if the equipment is used ASA (90% or more) of its operating time in the taxation year for SR&ED in Canada, 100% of the lease cost is claimable under both the Traditional and Proxy methods.

If the leased equipment is used primarily (more than 50% to less than 90%) for SR&ED, 50% of the lease cost (excluding GPOEF) is claimable under the Proxy Method (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(VI)), whereas under the Traditional Method the proportional percentage of operating time (<90%) is claimed as overhead on Line 360 if directly related and incremental. Lease costs for equipment used 50% or less cannot be claimed under the Proxy Method, and lease costs for buildings (other than prescribed special-purpose buildings under Regulation 2903) remain excluded under both methods.

body.text: Section 4: Government Assistance, Contract Payments, and Grant Stacking
4.1 Statutory Reduction Rules (ITA s. 37(1)(d), s. 127(11.1), s. 127(18)–(20))

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) (for the deductible pool) and subsections 127(11.1), 127(18), and 127(19) (for qualified expenditures), SR&ED claims are reduced dollar-for-dollar by any government assistance, non-government assistance (paragraph 12(1)(x) inducements/reimbursements), or contract payments in respect of SR&ED that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the filing-due date of its income tax return for the taxation year.

"Government assistance" (subsection 127(9)) encompasses any grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, or allowance from a government, municipality, Crown corporation, or public authority (excluding the federal SR&ED ITC). Importantly, if a government loan or contribution has conditional repayment terms—such as repayments dependent on future project revenues or capped royalties without firm, unconditional repayment schedules—the CRA treats the funding as government assistance that reduces the SR&ED pool and qualified expenditures immediately, rather than a business loan. When assistance is later repaid, the repayment increases the section 37 pool (paragraph 37(1)(c), Line 445) and section 127 qualified expenditures (Line 560) in the year repaid, earning an ITC at the rate that applied when the assistance originally reduced the claim. Non-arm's length parties may allocate assistance among group members using Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length).

Provincial and territorial R&D tax credits constitute government assistance that reduces federal SR&ED claims unless formally renounced or waived on or before the income tax return filing-due date. Under the Proxy Method, the portion of a provincial R&D tax credit that relates to the notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) does reduce section 127 qualified expenditures (subsection 127(18)), but does not reduce the section 37 deductible pool (paragraph 37(1)(d)) because the PPA is not in the pool; instead, the PPA-related portion of the provincial credit is included directly in income under paragraph 12(1)(x) in the year received or applied.

body.text: 4.3 Worked Mathematical Models of Multi-Program Stacking
Model A: Federal SR&ED + Ontario OITC (8%) + Ontario ORDTC (3.5%) Cascade Grind

When a qualifying CCPC with a permanent establishment in Ontario incurs CA$1,000,000 of qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures, the statutory order of operations under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario) and subsection 127(18) of the federal Income Tax Act proceeds in three sequential steps:

items: Step 1 — Calculate the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Schedule 566): Calculated first at 8% on the CA$1,000,000 qualified expenditure base (up to the CA$3,000,000 Ontario expenditure limit): OITC = 8% × CA$1,000,000 = CA$80,000 (Refundable Cash).

Step 2 — Calculate the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Schedule 508): Calculated second at 3.5% on the expenditure base net of the OITC (CA$1,000,000 − CA$80,000 = CA$920,000): ORDTC = 3.5% × CA$920,000 = CA$32,200 (Non-Refundable Ontario Tax Credit).

Step 3 — Calculate the Federal SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (Schedule T2SCH31): Both the CA$80,000 OITC and the CA$32,200 ORDTC reduce the federal qualified expenditure base on Line 513 of Form T661 (CA$1,000,000 − CA$80,000 − CA$32,200 = CA$887,800): Federal Enhanced ITC = 35% × CA$887,800 = CA$310,730 (Refundable Cash).

body.text: Combining all three credits yields CA$422,930 in total tax credits (42.293% effective rate, representing a net addition of CA$72,930 over a standalone CA$350,000 federal claim), of which CA$390,730 (39.073%) is immediate refundable cash (CA$80,000 OITC + CA$310,730 Federal ITC). If a loss-making corporation cannot utilize the non-refundable ORDTC and waives it by its filing due date, only the CA$80,000 OITC reduces the federal base (CA$1,000,000 − CA$80,000 = CA$920,000), yielding 35% × CA$920,000 = CA$322,000 federally plus CA$80,000 OITC for CA$402,000 (40.20%) in immediate refundable cash.
Model B: Clean Tech R&D Project Stacking NRC IRAP + Federal SR&ED + Clean Technology ITC

On a CA$500,000 clean technology R&D project comprising CA$250,000 in eligible R&D labour, CA$200,000 in eligible clean-energy capital equipment purchases, and CA$50,000 in other qualifying R&D expenses (plus proxy overhead), routing each expenditure to its optimal instrument yields the following stack:

items: NRC IRAP Contribution: Covers 80% of the CA$250,000 eligible R&D labour = CA$200,000 non-repayable grant.
Clean Technology ITC: Covers 30% of the CA$200,000 capital equipment purchase = CA$60,000 refundable tax credit.

Federal SR&ED Enhanced ITC: Applied at 35% to the CA$237,500 of qualified expenditures remaining after the IRAP assistance is subtracted (CA$250,000 R&D labour + CA$50,000 other R&D expenses + CA$137,500 PPA at 55% of the CA$250,000 salary base − CA$200,000 IRAP assistance) = CA$83,125 refundable tax credit.

body.text: Total non-dilutive recovery equals CA$343,125 (CA$200,000 + CA$60,000 + CA$83,125), reducing the company's net out-of-pocket cost on the CA$500,000 project to CA$156,875 (68.6% covered).

body.text: 5.2 Deep-Dive Analysis of Key Provincial Regimes
1. Québec: Transition from Legacy R&D Credits to the CRIC (March 25, 2025 Reform)

In its 2025–2026 Budget Plan delivered on March 25, 2025, the Québec government enacted a structural consolidation of Québec's innovation tax incentives, committing CA$2,412.6 million over five years (2025–2026 to 2029–2030, representing CA$271.5 million in net additional support after abolishing legacy measures) to establish the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) as the pillar of Québec's tax assistance system for innovation.

Effective for corporate taxation years (or partnership fiscal periods) beginning after March 25, 2025, Québec abolished eight legacy tax measures: (1–4) the four R&D tax credits for salaries and wages (Form RD-1029.7), university/public research centre/consortium research (Form RD-1029.8.6), private partnership pre-competitive research (Form RD-1029.8.16.1), and consortium fees and dues (Form RD-1029.8.9.03); (5) the industrial design component of the in-house (Form CO-1029.8.36.7) and outside consultant (Form CO-1029.8.36.5) design credits; (6) the tax credit for technological adaptation services; (7) the tax holiday for hiring foreign researchers; and (8) the tax holiday for hiring foreign experts.

Under the new CRIC regime (Form RD-1029.8.CR, with associated-group limit allocation on Form RD-1029.8.EN and SR&ED deduction reporting on Form RD-222), eligible activities encompass both R&D activities and pre-commercialization activities (such as product design that constitutes a continuation of an R&D project carried out in Québec). Eligible CRIC expenditures include salaries and wages, capital expenditures for the acquisition of equipment/property, and 50% of the value of contracts entered into with subcontractors, universities, public research centres, or research consortia. Crucially, CRIC rates do not vary by business size: every eligible corporation earns a 100% refundable credit of 30% on the first CA$1,000,000 of eligible expenditures in excess of its annual exclusion threshold, and 20% on eligible expenditures above that CA$1,000,000 limit. The annual exclusion threshold equals the higher of (a) CA$50,000 or (b) the sum of the employee-specific exclusion amounts, where each employee's threshold equals the basic personal amount under the Québec personal income tax system (CA$18,571 in 2025) adjusted to the proportion of their time spent carrying out eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities.
2. Ontario: Capital Harmonization vs. Expenditure Cap Divergence
Auditors reviewing Ontario claims for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, must verify two critical rules governing the interaction of Ontario and federal SR&ED incentives:

First, while federal Bill C-15 raised the federal enhanced 35% expenditure limit to CA$6.0 million, Ontario left the 8% OITC expenditure limit at CA$3,000,000 of qualified Ontario expenditures (maximum CA$240,000 credit, shared among associated corporations). Furthermore, the OITC retains its provincial phase-outs between CA$500,000 and CA$800,000 of prior-year federal taxable income and between CA$25,000,000 and CA$50,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital. Consequently, spending between CA$3.0 million and CA$6.0 million earns the federal 35% enhanced ITC but not the 8% OITC on a CA$6.0 million claim.

Second, Ontario matched the federal restoration of capital property for both the OITC and the ORDTC: 100% of qualified capital expenditures made on or after December 16, 2024, qualify in Ontario (with provincial assistance on capital property reported on Line 514 of Form T661), whereas capital property acquired between January 1, 2014, and December 15, 2024, remains ineligible.
3. Alberta and Saskatchewan: Incremental and Expanded Western Incentives

In Alberta, the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) (sections 26.95 to 26.99 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act, claimed on AT1 Schedule 29 and Form AT4970) provides a refundable grant equal to 8% of eligible Alberta R&D spending up to the corporation's base level of spending (the average qualifying Alberta R&D spending over the preceding 2 years) plus an enhanced 20% payment on eligible Alberta R&D spending exceeding that 2-year base average, on up to CA$4,000,000 in annual R&D spending, phasing out for taxable capital between CA$10 million and CA$50 million.

In Saskatchewan, under sections 63 to 63.4 of The Income Tax Act, 2000 (Saskatchewan) and T2 Schedule 403, CCPCs earn a 10% refundable credit on the first CA$2,000,000 of eligible expenditures for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (doubled from the CA$1,000,000 limit for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024), while non-CCPCs and CCPC expenditures above the refundable limit earn a 10% non-refundable credit, subject to an overall annual credit cap of CA$1,000,000.
Section 6: Governing Bodies, Pre-Claim Approval, Filing Procedures, Prescribed Forms, and Penalties
6.1 Governing Authorities and Administrative Division of Labour
Canada's federal SR&ED program is governed through two federal institutions:

items: Department of Finance Canada: Responsible for tax policy formulation and legislative amendments to the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations.
Canada Revenue Agency (CRA): Administers the SR&ED program through specialized SR&ED Coordinating Tax Services Offices (CTSOs) staffed by two distinct specialist roles:

Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs): Conduct the technical review to determine whether claimed projects meet the scientific or technological eligibility requirements of subsection 248(1), reporting to a Research and Technology Manager (RTM).

Financial Reviewers (FRs): Conduct the financial review to determine whether claimed expenditures, proxy calculations, and assistance adjustments comply with sections 37 and 127, reporting to a Financial Review Manager (FRM).

body.text: 6.2 The Optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026)

Launched by the CRA on April 1, 2026, the optional Pre-Claim Approval Process allows eligible businesses to have their planned R&D projects evaluated to confirm whether they meet SR&ED technical requirements before beginning work or incurring significant costs (or if work has only recently begun).

To qualify for Pre-Claim Approval, the business and project must meet five mandatory criteria: (1) the business must be a CCPC, another Canadian corporation, or a Canadian partnership; (2) the business must have annual gross business income of less than CA$25,000,000; (3) the business must be in good standing with the CRA; (4) the application may cover up to 3 projects, none of which has been included in a previous SR&ED claim; and (5) the projects must not involve issues currently under litigation.
The application proceeds through four sequential steps using Form T1322 (Application for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Pre-Claim Approval):

items: Step 1 — Request a Case Number: The business completes a web form (taking under five minutes) with its contact details and 15-character Business Number. The CRA provides a case number within 2 business days via My Business Account for existing SR&ED claimants in good standing, or within 5 business days by telephone for all other businesses.

Step 2 — Complete Form T1322 and Gather Supporting Documents: For each project (up to 3), the applicant completes Part 2 of Form T1322, including three technical narratives subject to strict word limits: Line 042 (Maximum 500 words) describing the scientific or technological uncertainty aimed to be addressed; Line 043 (Maximum 700 words) detailing the due diligence completed (literature, patents, standards, expert consultations, and preliminary trials) confirming that existing knowledge cannot resolve the uncertainty; and Line 044 (Maximum 900 words) describing the hypotheses, experiments/analyses, and external contractors planned over the pre-claim approval period (up to 3 years). Section D requires four categories of supporting documents (up to 10 uploaded files): (a) project planning documents (timelines, milestones, Gantt charts, work breakdown structures); (b) a description of planned internal controls (time-tracking processes, experimental record-keeping protocols); (c) key supporting due-diligence references (scientific articles, design specifications, system architecture diagrams, photographs); and (d) a list of prospective project team members with their credentials and expertise. All files must be uploaded in a single session via "Submit documents" in My Business Account.

Step 3 — Meet with a CRA SR&ED Specialist (Within 4 Weeks): Within 4 weeks of submitting the application, a CRA SR&ED specialist contacts the business to hold a technical meeting (mandatory for new SR&ED claimants; discretionary for existing claimants in good standing).

Step 4 — Receive Official Determination (Within 8 Weeks): Within 8 weeks of completing the application in My Business Account, the CRA issues an official Pre-Claim Approval determination valid for up to 3 years. When the claimant subsequently files Form T661, it checks Line 212 and enters the case number on Line 214; if a claim containing only pre-approved projects is selected for an expenditure-only review, the CRA's processing service standard is cut in half from 180 calendar days to 90 calendar days.

body.text: 6.3 The Absolute 18-Month Statutory Reporting Deadline

Under subsection 37(11) and paragraph 127(9)(m) of the Income Tax Act, a taxpayer's SR&ED reporting deadline is 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred. For corporations (whose T2 filing-due date under paragraph 150(1)(a) is 6 months after taxation year-end), the SR&ED reporting deadline is 18 months after the end of the taxation year. For individuals (whose T1 filing-due date is April 30, or June 15 for self-employed individuals), the reporting deadline is 12 months after that filing-due date (17.5 months after year-end for self-employed individuals). For trusts (whose T3 filing-due date is 90 days after year-end), the reporting deadline is 12 months plus 90 days after year-end. For partnerships, Form T661 must be filed at the partnership level, while each partner files Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND) by their respective corporate or individual SR&ED reporting deadline.

Under subsection 220(2.2) of the Act, the CRA is prohibited by law from extending the 18-month reporting deadline (subsection 220(3.1) taxpayer relief cannot be used to extend it). Under the SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy and subsection 37(12), if Form T661 is filed after the 18-month reporting deadline, the claim is rejected in full and the expenditures are statutorily precluded from being deducted under section 37 or earning an ITC under section 127. If Form T661 is filed on time with all prescribed information, but Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND) is filed after the 18-month deadline, the expenditures may be added to the section 37 deductible pool, but the claimant forfeits 100% of the section 127 ITC.

body.text: 6.5 Statutory Penalty Regimes (ITA s. 162(5.1)–(5.3), s. 163(2), and s. 163.2)

Under subsections 162(5.1) to 162(5.3) of the Income Tax Act, a CA$1,000 penalty applies for each SR&ED claim for which prescribed information in Part 9 of Form T661 regarding the claim preparer(s) is missing, incomplete, or inaccurate. If a claim preparer (defined as any person or partnership accepting consideration to prepare or assist in preparing Form T661, excluding an employee acting in the course of employment duties) prepared or assisted in preparing the claim, the claim preparer is jointly and severally, or solidarily, liable with the claimant for the CA$1,000 penalty, subject to the due-diligence defence in subsection 162(5.2). Missing or incomplete Part 9 information does not disallow the underlying SR&ED claim at the 18-month reporting deadline.

Under subsection 163(2) of the Act and the CRA's Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy (updated January 28, 2025), if a claimant knowingly, or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence, makes or participates in a false statement or omission on an original or amended SR&ED claim, the civil penalty is the greater of CA$100 or 50% of the total of: (1) the understated Part I tax payable reasonably attributable to the false statement or omission (paragraph 163(2)(a), where overstated section 37 pool deductions and overstated ITC deductions are considered deducted first, and loss-making corporations are deemed to have taxable income not less than zero under subsection 163(2.1)); plus (2) the refund of the entire overstated refundable ITC claimed under subsection 127.1(1) (paragraph 163(2)(d)). Under subsection 163(3), the CRA bears the burden of establishing on a balance of probabilities that the false statement resulted from more than a simple oversight or misunderstanding of the Act. In addition, third-party preparers who make, furnish, or participate in false statements knowingly or under circumstances amounting to culpable conduct are subject to third-party civil penalties under section 163.2 (Information Circular IC01-1).
6.6 Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credits (ITA subsections 127(27) to 127(36))

Under the CRA's Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy and subsections 127(27) to 127(36) of the Act, an SR&ED ITC is recaptured (added directly to Part I federal tax payable in the year, and increasing the section 37 deductible pool in the following year under paragraph 37(1)(c.2) / Line 453) when all four statutory conditions are met:

items: The claimant acquired a particular property in the current taxation year or in any of the 20 preceding taxation years (subsection 127(36));

The cost of the property (materials transformed, post-December 15, 2024 ASA capital property, Shared-Use Equipment, animals/plants, or property acquired through an SR&ED contract) was a qualified SR&ED expenditure;
The cost was included in computing the claimant's ITC at the end of a taxation year; and
The claimant disposes of the property (or another property that incorporates it) or converts it to commercial use in the taxation year.

body.text: Salaries, wages, and overhead never trigger ITC recapture, and materials consumed or scrap sales do not trigger recapture under a de minimis administrative rule where proceeds of disposition or fair market value upon commercial conversion are less than 10% of the total cost of the property.
Section 7: Judicial Precedents, CRA Review Methodology, and Audit Defence Framework
7.1 The CRA Two-Step Administrative Framework ("Why" and "How") vs. The Judicial Five-Question Test
In its Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives (issued August 13, 2021), the CRA frames technical eligibility around a Two-Step Approach:

items: The "Why" Requirement: Work must be conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving technological advancement—specifically generating or discovering conceptual knowledge (theories, principles, or prediction models) required because of a scientific or technological uncertainty (an insufficiency in the combined publicly available and internal knowledge base).

The "How" Requirement: Work must be a systematic investigation or search carried out by means of experiment or analysis, comprising four mandatory steps: (a) defining a problem and advancing a hypothesis (idea or proposed solution); (b) testing the hypothesis through experiment or analysis; (c) developing logical conclusions based on the results; and (d) keeping evidence generated as the work progresses.

body.text: As the Federal Court of Appeal definitively ruled in National R&D Inc. v. Canada (2022 FCA 72) and Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada (2021 FCA 88), CRA administrative guidelines are not legally binding on the courts; rather, Canadian courts are bound by legal precedent and the Five-Question Test established in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen (98 D.T.C. 1839):

items: Question 1 (Technological Risk or Uncertainty): Was there a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures?
Question 2 (Formulation of Hypotheses): Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty?
Question 3 (Scientific Method): Did the procedure adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses?
Question 4 (Technological Advancement): Did the process result in a technological advancement?
Question 5 (Detailed Record-Keeping): Was a detailed record of the hypotheses tested, and results kept as the work progressed?

body.text: 7.2 Landmark Canadian SR&ED Jurisprudence
The table below synthesizes the foundational decisions of the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) and Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) governing SR&ED claims:

cells: Meaning of "systematic investigation or search" and documentary proof.

Held that "systematic investigation" requires controlled, repeatable experiments, accurate measurements, and the testing of theories against empirical evidence where steps, changes, and results are carefully noted. Claim failed because the taxpayer provided no overall project descriptions, drawings, test reports, or evidence of a hypothesis.
Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen 98 D.T.C. 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520
Tax Court of Canada (May 1, 1998 — Bowman J.T.C.C.)
Foundational judicial test for SR&ED eligibility and definition of "routine engineering".

Articulated the Five-Question Test. Defined "routine engineering" as techniques, procedures, and data generally accessible to competent professionals in the field, and held that maintaining detailed records of hypotheses, tests, and results as the work progresses is self-evident.
RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen 99 D.T.C. 5087, [1998] F.C.J. No. 1890
Appellate endorsement of Northwest Hydraulic; eligibility of failed research; repeatability inference.

Adopted the Northwest Hydraulic five criteria at the appellate level. Held that failed R&D projects qualify for SR&ED because the statute requires only that work be undertaken for the purpose of advancement, not that it actually achieve that end. Held that once testing and technological advancement are proven, an inference arises that testing was systematic without requiring separate documentary proof of repeatability.
C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada 2001 FCA 393 (aff'g 2000 D.T.C. 2372 TCC)
Federal Court of Appeal (Dec 11, 2001 — Sexton J.A.)
Software development eligibility; weight of retroactive expert reconstruction vs. contemporaneous records.

Upheld disallowance of software development claims for a multi-language lottery computer system. Held that after-the-fact conjecture by an outside expert attempting to reconstruct problems and steps from final results and tools—without contemporaneous project plans or testimony from project managers—is insufficient.
Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen 2011 TCC 261, aff'd 2011 FCA 355
Tax Court of Canada & Federal Court of Appeal (2011 — D'Arcy J.)
Sufficiency of proving a "systematic investigation" without proving technological uncertainty; Statement of Agreed Facts (SAF) risks.

Dismissed claim for moulded plastic modular storage bins. Held that although the SAF established that Jentel conducted a documented systematic investigation, the claim failed because the SAF focused on improving product form without proving technological uncertainty or why existing manufacturing processes/materials failed (routine engineering). Also gave zero weight to the CRA science advisor's opinion testimony because he was not qualified as an expert witness.
Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen 2017 TCC 6
Applied mechanics; distinction between "systematic investigation" and "trial and error"; team qualifications.

Upheld disallowance of a motorized hydraulic theatre fire-curtain control device as "routine engineering" and "trial and error" because the team included no professional engineers or degreed researchers, formulated no specific hypotheses across iterations, and failed to measure exact weights or descent durations. Noted that while contemporaneous records may not be an absolute prerequisite in all cases, their absence was fatal here.
Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada 2021 FCA 88
Statutory relocation of SR&ED definition from ITR s. 2900 to ITA s. 248(1).
Confirmed that moving the SR&ED definition to subsection 248(1) did not alter the law, and the Northwest Hydraulic five-part test remains the proper legal interpretation.
National R&D Inc. v. Canada 2022 FCA 72 (aff'g 2020 TCC 47 / 2020 TCC 67)
Federal Court of Appeal (May 2022 — Rennie J.A.)
Mandatory nature of the "scientific method" criterion; CRA guidelines vs. case law; disqualification of tainted expert witnesses.

Held that: (1) meeting Question 1 (technological uncertainty) alone is insufficient when Questions 2–5 fail; (2) the Northwest Hydraulic criteria are valid judicial interpretation under Canada Trustco (2005 SCC 54) and are not overridden by revised CRA guidelines omitting the phrase "scientific method"; (3) any alleged distinction between "engineering method" and "scientific method" must be proven by expert evidence at trial; and (4) an external expert witness report must be excluded where the taxpayer wrote 65% of the report, the tone was advocacy, and the report opined on domestic law.

body.text: 7.3 CRA SR&ED Review Process, Audit Defence Protocols, and Dispute Resolution

When an SR&ED claim is selected for review, the CRA follows the three-step procedure set out in The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants (updated April 20, 2026) and the Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors:

items: Step 1 — The Start of the Review and 30-Day Information Request: An assigned reviewer (RTA or FR) contacts the claimant by phone to introduce the RTA and FR, confirm the official language of choice, identify the specific issues and projects under review, and schedule a virtual (or, exceptionally, on-site) review meeting. An initial letter follows summarizing the call, providing a meeting agenda, and listing any information requested prior to the meeting under the Standard Timelines for Information Requests (generally 30 days). The CRA's service standard for processing refundable SR&ED claims selected for review is 180 calendar days from receipt of a complete claim (or 90 calendar days for an expenditure-only review of a claim granted Pre-Claim Approval).

Step 2 — The Review Meeting, Interviews, Tour, and Supporting Evidence (ITA s. 230(1) and s. 230(4)(b)): During the review meeting, the RTA and FR interview the individuals who directly performed or supervised the work to examine the shortcomings of existing knowledge at the start of the project, chronological hypotheses, experiments/analyses, and failures or problems encountered along the way. Oral statements during interviews are considered, but oral statements are not a substitute for keeping adequate contemporaneous documentation (such as dated documents, photographs, videos, physical samples, scrap, software revision logs, or commit logs supporting Lines 270–282 of Form T661, and financial ledgers, journals, vouchers, and contracts kept in electronically readable format for at least 6 years under subsection 230(1) and paragraph 230(4)(b)). During a virtual or on-site premises tour, the RTA inspects ASA capital equipment, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) and usage logs, prototypes, pilot plants, and scrap yards. Under Section 5.10.0 of the Claim Review Manual, RTAs are strictly prohibited from negotiating eligibility or swapping project approvals, though once eligibility is proven, reviewers may use objective estimation bases where boundaries are imprecise.

Step 3 — Review Findings, Dispute Resolution, and Formal Notice of Objection: At the end of the review meeting, reviewers share preliminary findings and set a deadline for any missing information before issuing a written review report. Under Section 5.2.0 of the Claim Review Manual, the RTA must consult the Research and Technology Manager (RTM) before recommending disallowance due to lack of information, issuing an unfavourable decision without a site visit, or applying penalties. If a claimant disagrees with the reviewers' findings, it can escalate concerns through the CRA's administrative dispute resolution process (from the RTA/FR to the RTM/FRM). If the dispute remains unresolved and the CRA issues a Notice of Assessment or Reassessment, the claimant has the statutory right to file a formal Notice of Objection within 90 days from the date of the Notice of Assessment or Reassessment, with a further right of appeal to the Tax Court of Canada and the Federal Court of Appeal.
